title: Offering sips, ice, or no pressure around food and fluids

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source practice-layer synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: Public sources describe recognized care patterns but do not supply firsthand room texture.
This record must not become procedure-level instruction for a particular death.
Treatment, legal, ritual, emergency, and equipment decisions remain local and must be handled by qualified teams or relevant authorities.

moment.plain_scene: A family member wants to feed or give water because that has always meant care, while the dying person eats little, drinks little, coughs, refuses, or cannot safely swallow.
ordinary_language_queries: should I force water when someone is dying
food and drink end of life guilt
not eating or drinking near death

content_layers.observation_text: Public and professional sources describe reduced intake near death and warn that fluid/feeding decisions are context-specific; they commonly emphasize comfort, mouth care, and not pressuring the person to eat or drink.
content_layers.source_synthesis: The source set supports a cautious record: food and fluid are emotionally charged, clinically variable, and must not be turned into one-size-fits-all instruction.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: This is a moral-distress record. The scene is not only “not drinking”; it is “I love them and the old language of love no longer works.”

what_this_is_not: not a command to stop or start food, fluids, artificial hydration, or medication
not a judgment on families who want to feed
not a universal rule for every illness, culture, or legal setting
not evidence that a particular person is or is not thirsty
uncertainties: Artificial hydration and swallowing safety need individualized assessment.
VSED, eating disorders, pediatric dying, dementia care, and religious water practices require separate high-gate treatment.
Future records should preserve family phrases like “starving,” “giving up,” and “letting die” with care.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should meet feeding guilt directly and distinguish comfort from forcing. It should advise readers with specific worries to contact their hospice or clinical team.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect how experienced workers explain reduced intake without making families feel they are abandoning the person.
language_notes: Keep “starving” as a search term, not a default explanation.
Avoid “the body knows” as a totalizing phrase.
Use “pressure” carefully: do not blame families.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the practice layer. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, not a legal instruction, not a ritual authority, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, legal, cultural, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical or domain review and ensure any lay surface directs urgent, worried, legal, medication, swallowing, equipment, or body-handling questions to qualified local support.
